description: Hire Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2025.

talks.title: The World Famous Hire Ground Panel, Tuesday Edition
talks.teaser: Recruiters, hiring managers and community managers discuss ghosting, degree requirements, job market trends and résumé advice.
talks.summary:
This village panel brings together recruiters and hiring staff from agency, corporate, government contracting and community management roles. They open by explaining how each type of recruiter shapes a candidate's experience, and why agency and internal recruiters often have different access to job details and clients.

The conversation then turns to candidate frustrations. Panelists discuss being ghosted after applications and interviews, and why recruiters often lack client feedback. They describe degree and certification requirements as filters that can sometimes be waived, and point out that many listings are reposted across boards, sometimes by scraping sites. Advice on résumés centres on tailoring each one to the specific role and stating concrete recent work. Several panelists say referrals, direct outreach to recruiters and networking account for most of their successful hires, and they warn about fake recruiter profiles and automated applications.

Near the end, the group reviews the market, noting strong demand for experienced people alongside fewer entry-level roles, and suggests staying open to contract or adjacent work. Panelists also name critical infrastructure, energy and embedded security as areas with hiring needs, and the audience questions cover AI in screening and candidate use of AI tools. The main takeaway is to be specific about what you have done, follow up persistently, and build relationships rather than relying on job boards alone.

talks.title: From Help Desk to CISO
talks.teaser: Maps a route from help desk work to security leadership, with the non-technical skills that carry people up the ladder.
talks.summary:
Many people in IT support wonder how to reach security leadership, and this career talk lays out a route from the help desk to a CISO role. The speaker argues that the job market still has room for newcomers outside large tech firms, and that the standard career frameworks show a tidy linear progression that real careers rarely follow. He notes that support and networking roles are valid entry points and that moving sideways or back is normal.

The talk traces his own path through retail and automotive jobs, where he picked up customer service and troubleshooting, then help desk, networking, security administration, election-systems auditing and a state CISO post. He describes how a stint as a technology leader shifted his work toward budgets and crisis calls, which led him back to a more hands-on technical management role. He treats certifications as a way to clear non-technical screening, while experience is what earns the next job.

The closing advice focuses on skills rather than degrees: translating technical work into risk and dollar terms, using metrics for board conversations, practicing storytelling and public speaking, building local networks and mentors, and volunteering for small leadership tasks. He ends by saying a CISO is one option among several, and that engineering or architecture paths can be a better fit and help avoid burnout.

talks.title: Beyond the Command Line: Transitioning from Individual Contributor to Leader
talks.teaser: Explains how strong technical staff can move into leadership roles without losing their footing.
talks.summary:
Many security professionals are promoted into management because they are strong technical contributors, yet few receive preparation for the new job. The talk describes this as a leadership gap and links it to burnout, citing a survey in which many security staff reported higher job stress than five years earlier. The speaker argues that moving into leadership is a career change, where success shifts from personal output to enabling a team.

The middle of the talk covers four core skills: communication tailored to each audience, delegation without micromanagement, decision-making under pressure, and giving and receiving feedback. It then addresses leading former peers, recommending a direct conversation about the new reporting line, written role expectations, and consistent treatment to avoid perceived favoritism. Imposter syndrome and the habit of staying too technical are also discussed, with advice to seek feedback from peers, managers and direct reports.

The question round covered delegating work without lowering quality, keeping technical skills current, and whether to seek management at all. The closing message is that leadership is defined by a change in focus rather than a job title, and that people should choose it deliberately, with honest conversations about their motivation.

talks.title: No Slides, Just Vibes
talks.teaser: Gives job seekers practical advice on resumes, interview preparation, and asking good questions during hiring.
talks.summary:
This career session is aimed at people looking for security jobs. The speaker draws on his experience as a threat intelligence hiring manager and as someone who has changed jobs often. He argues that many candidates spend too much effort on their resume and too little preparing for the interview, where hiring managers quickly judge both technical ability and fit.

Much of the talk covers preparation. He recommends rehearsing a short, tailored introduction, building a few stories that map to likely technical and non-technical questions, showing enthusiasm without overdoing nerves, and answering weakness questions with a mitigation. Resume advice includes tailoring each version to the role, keeping it to one or two pages with the key facts on page one, leaving out unrelated hobbies and old jobs, and staying active on LinkedIn. Audience questions covered employment gaps, career changers, cover letters, expired certifications, and handling curveball questions from a poorly prepared interviewer.

He closes by urging candidates to ask two or three specific questions, such as day-to-day duties, how performance and promotions work, and who the actual decision maker is, since those questions help separate candidates. He also warns against paying for resume reviews and points to free career village help and recruiters. The takeaway is that a prepared candidate who treats the process as a two-way evaluation stands out.

talks.title: Root To CISO or not?
talks.teaser: Four career-path questions get answered by CISOs and a recruiter, covering routes into leadership and avoiding burnout.
talks.summary:
A panel of two multi-time CISOs and a recruiter takes audience questions about how security leaders reach their roles. The discussion opens with each panelist's background, from technical operations work to an unconventional first security job, and the moderator frames the session around practical career decisions.

Much of the middle focuses on leading with limited budgets and staying technical. Panelists suggested building trust with engineering teams, partnering with early-stage startups, and keeping staff connected to the mission. They agreed the role shifts toward finance, business strategy and communicating risk, though many leaders keep hands-on skills. Certifications drew skepticism compared with demonstrated ability, and metrics such as risk reduction, return on investment and measured employee competence were proposed for reporting upward. Vendor questionnaires were criticized as weak evidence of real controls.

The closing advice centers on hiring well, defending the team, choosing a manager who advances your career and telling your own story clearly. Internal promotion was described as the most reliable route to a CISO job, since outside applicants face a crowded market.

talks.title: Your Interview Game is Weak: Gamifying Technical Interviews through Role-Playing
talks.teaser: Shows how role-playing interview exercises can assess job-relevant skills better than rote technical challenges.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many technical interviews test the wrong things. The speaker, an application security manager with a development background, cites published data and an informal survey of security engineers. The findings included poor candidate experience, interview content that often did not match the job, arbitrary challenges, memorized definitions, and processes that ran for five or more hours. Skills missing from the job posting were frequently ignored, and interview formats sometimes punished candidates who used tools they would use on the job.

To address this, the speaker built a role-playing interview kit set in a fictional skateboarding-themed security startup. Candidates work through about four job-relevant challenges, such as threat modeling, code review, a secrets management decision, and a penetration test of an open-source tool. Interviewers take on non-player characters with motivations, alliances, and budget concerns, so responses vary and rote preparation is less effective. Candidates receive the materials in advance, and the kit is meant to be adapted to a team's own context rather than copied.

The speaker reported that after the second version of the kit was used for a hire, the process took two months instead of six, the candidate pool shrank fivefold, and several candidates gave positive feedback. Advice for hiring teams included investing time in the process, involving stakeholders from adjacent teams, and assessing both technical and interpersonal skills. Advice for candidates included volunteering, speaking, seeking mentorship, and asking questions during interviews.

talks.title: Hack Your Network: Career Connections for Cyber Pros
talks.teaser: Shows cybersecurity professionals how relationships built through events, LinkedIn and mentorship can open career doors.
talks.summary:
Heather Morris, a recruiting director in the government contracting talent space, opens by arguing that networking is a core career skill for security people. The field changes quickly, and many roles are filled through referrals and word of mouth rather than open applications. Good contacts keep you informed about job openings and industry trends, bring you collaborators, and give you access to mentors and shared knowledge.

The middle of the talk is practical. Before an event, decide what you want from it, whether that is learning, meeting peers or finding work, and prepare a short introduction covering who you are and what you are looking for. Research the speakers and attendees, then plan which sessions, booths and social gatherings to visit. During the event, approach conversations by asking how you can help or what you can learn, not what you can get. Afterwards, send personalized LinkedIn requests that mention something specific from the conversation, and keep up with people by engaging with their posts. Online, keep your profile current, comment thoughtfully, join relevant groups, follow hashtags, and build a personal brand through writing or public code. Morris also warns against pitching yourself too early, since it tends to come across as self-serving.

The talk closes with mentorship and long-term maintenance. A mentor can be someone you admire and follow, met at an event or on a stage, and an informal arrangement such as shadowing or feedback is often enough. Mentors also benefit from newer people who bring current skills. Relationships need regular check-ins, in-person time where possible, and help offered in return. Morris stresses authenticity, quality over quantity, and patience, since returns on networking rarely arrive quickly.

talks.title: Craps, Clout, and Career Chaos: The Game They Forgot to Explain
talks.teaser: Offers career advice for security professionals on communication, leadership, political capital and building allies.
talks.summary:
A career session that frames cybersecurity advancement as a game of craps, presented by two security leaders: a CISO with over 25 years in IT and a senior manager who leads a threat intelligence team. The speakers argue that technical skill alone does not move a career forward. They start with plain language over jargon, since boards will not fund programs they cannot follow, and recommend leading with the issue, its business importance and the specific ask in a short summary. They also urge people to bring proposed solutions rather than problems, and to learn how the business and its risk fit together, using public filings as a starting point.

The middle of the session covers working relationships. The presenters describe treating feedback as useful rather than personal, building allies across teams instead of only collecting contacts, and choosing which fights are worth spending political capital and energy on. They describe building teams that can run without the leader, and betting on yourself when a role looks slightly beyond reach. In the question period, the speakers said hiring managers often weigh drive and a clear reason for wanting the role above a full match with a job posting's requirements.

The takeaway is that career growth depends on communication, influence and relationships, and that patience matters because progress is slow. The session was delivered as a conversation with anecdotes from both leadership perspectives rather than a technical presentation.

talks.title: Where’s Waldo? Why Recruiters Can’t Find You (and What To Do About It)
talks.teaser: Shows how recruiters search LinkedIn and what makes a security professional's profile easier to find.
talks.summary:
The session opens by questioning why a professional networking profile exists and who actually looks at it. The speaker, an agency recruiter who places cybersecurity candidates, argues that the platform works as a hiring tool, so a person who cannot be found by recruiters misses opportunities, both immediate and later. The audience joins in by acting as recruiters for a live search for a penetration tester near Los Angeles, starting with job-title variants and keyword combinations, then narrowing a pool of more than a hundred results.

The group then reviews a sample profile as a recruiter would. Points raised include how little time a recruiter gives each profile, often well under a minute, and how vague titles such as security engineer leave readers guessing about the actual role. An about section adds human context, and certifications carry different weight depending on the employer, with government roles often valuing credentials that private firms do not. Visible activity, such as posting about attending events, is presented as a way to build credibility, and a warm introduction from someone in the network can outweigh a cold application.

The practical takeaways are to decide which specialty you want to be known for, to use specific keywords and quantified outcomes rather than copied duty lists, and to keep resumes short and targeted. The question-and-answer segment covers whether Premium subscriptions and open-to-work banners help, how to handle career changers, and how far to tailor cover letters and use AI for that.
